technicalNotes.heading: What the boat has to be able to do
bullets: Self-righting when fully enclosed, with everyone strapped in.
Carries the number of persons marked on it, each with a seat, a seat belt and a lifejacket stowage.
Fire-protected boats on tankers carry the water spray (sprinkler) system and the air support system, and can run through a fire on the water for the required period.
The engine starts and runs the boat at not less than 6 knots for the required period, and runs out of the water for the time the maker states — normally 5 minutes.

technicalNotes.heading: The weekly and monthly regime
bullets: Weekly: start the engine and run it for at least 3 minutes (SOLAS III/20.6.2) — with the boat's own cooling water supply where the arrangement needs it, or the engine will overheat.
Weekly: operate the general emergency alarm, and inspect the boat, davits, falls and release gear visually.
Monthly: a full inspection of the boat against the checklist, including the equipment inventory, confirmed in the log.

Every three months: lower the boat to the embarkation deck where the arrangement allows. Every three months a crew enters and manoeuvres a boat in the water, unless the ship's arrangement makes it impracticable.

technicalNotes.heading: Inventory items that get written up
bullets: Buoyant oars, boat hooks, bailer and buckets, survival manual, compass, sea anchor with hawser and tripping line.
Painters — two, one at the forward end with a release arrangement, one secured at or near the bow.
Fire extinguisher, torch with spare batteries, signalling mirror, whistle, first-aid outfit, seasickness bags and tablets.
Pyrotechnics: four rocket parachute flares, six hand flares, two buoyant smoke signals — all in date.
Fresh water at 3 litres per person, food rations, drinking vessel, fishing tackle, jack-knife, tin opener, thermal protective aids.
Rations and water carry an expiry date and are the most commonly out-of-date item in the boat.

technicalNotes.heading: What is different about a free-fall boat
bullets: It is launched by falling from a stern ramp, so the certification covers the boat, the ramp and the acceleration on the occupants together.
Every seat is designed for the free-fall load, and the seat belts and head restraints are part of the structure, not comfort items.
There is a secondary means of launching — normally a davit — because a free-fall launch cannot be used for routine drills.
The release is operated from inside the boat by the coxswain.

technicalNotes.heading: Drills without launching it
bullets: SOLAS III/19.3.3.4: the free-fall boat is either free-fall launched with only the operating crew on board, or lowered into the water by the secondary means, at intervals not exceeding three months.
Where a free-fall launch is not carried out, a simulated launching is done at intervals not exceeding six months, in accordance with MSC.1/Circ.1206.
Both are logged, and the log entry says which was done. 'Boat inspected' does not satisfy either.
Before any launch: the release gear, the ramp, the hydraulic system and the securing arrangement are checked, and the area astern is clear.

helpTextEn: On-load release gear — the fwd and aft hooks, the operating linkage and the hydrostatic interlock. Only a provider authorised for this make and type may carry out the annual examination and the five-yearly overload test.
commonPscFindings: Five-yearly overload test overdue

technicalNotes.heading: Why this equipment has its own IMO resolution
bullets: On-load release gear releases a lifeboat's hooks under the full load of the boat. It has killed more seafarers in drills than almost any other item of LSA, which is why MSC.402(96) made servicing a certified activity.
MSC.402(96) requires an annual thorough examination and operational test, and a five-yearly overload operational test.
The five-yearly test is done at 1.1 times the total mass of the boat with its full complement and equipment.
Only a manufacturer, or a service provider certified by the manufacturer and authorised by the Administration, may do the annual and five-yearly work — the ship's staff cannot sign it off.

technicalNotes.heading: What the ship's staff do check
bullets: Hook setting: the cam or locking arrangement fully home, the indicator showing set, and the safety pin in place with its seal where the design has one.
The interlock that prevents on-load release while the boat is out of the water.
Free movement of the operating linkage, and no corrosion or wasted pins.
The hydrostatic interlock is not a substitute for the safety pin: both exist, and both are checked.
Never operate the on-load release with people in the boat. Recovery and lowering drills are done with the boat unmanned wherever the arrangement allows.

helpTextEn: Falls used in launching. Record the fitting date, the end-for-end date and the renewal date from the wire certificate — do not assume an interval, take it from SOLAS III/20 and the maker's manual.

technicalNotes.heading: Renewal — and the change people miss
bullets: SOLAS III/20.4 as amended: falls used in launching are inspected periodically, with special regard for areas passing through sheaves, and renewed when necessary due to deterioration or at intervals of not more than five years, whichever is earlier.
The older requirement to turn falls end-for-end at intervals not exceeding 30 months was removed by amendment — check which edition your ship's certificate is issued under before quoting either.
Renewal is by date or by condition, whichever comes first: a fall inside five years with broken wires at the sheave is condemned.
Record the date of renewal against the fall, not against the boat: the two falls of one boat can have different histories.

technicalNotes.heading: What to look at
bullets: The lengths that sit in a sheave when the boat is stowed: they carry the load, they never move, and they corrode from the inside.
Broken wires, especially at the terminations and at the drum's first layer.
Reduction in diameter, birdcaging, kinks and corrosion product weeping from between the strands.
The eye and the thimble at the hook, and the bulldog grips if the arrangement uses them — the correct number, the correct way round, and torqued.

helpTextEn: Throw-over inflatable liferaft in a GRP container. The float-free arrangement — HRU, painter and weak link — is the single most common finding on this item, so it is on the monthly checklist.
commonPscFindings: Servicing overdue or the servicing certificate not on board
HRU expired or the painter not rigged through the weak link

Raft stowed so it cannot float free; senhouse slip painted over

technicalNotes.heading: The float-free chain, end to end
bullets: Container, lashing with a slip hook or senhouse slip, cradle, painter, weak link, and the hydrostatic release unit — every link has to be right or the raft goes down with the ship.
The painter is made fast to the ship's structure through the weak link, never directly to a strong point that the raft cannot break away from.
Painter length: not less than 15 m, or the distance from the stowage position to the waterline in the lightest seagoing condition plus 10 m, whichever is the greater.
The weak link breaks at 2.0 ± 0.4 kN — strong enough to pull the painter and inflate the raft, weak enough to let the raft go as the ship sinks.
The HRU releases the lashing at a depth of not more than 4 m.

technicalNotes.heading: Inflation and capacity
bullets: Inflates fully within one minute at an ambient temperature of 18 to 20°C, and within three minutes at −30°C.
Capacity, SOLAS pack (A or B), servicing station and next service date are marked on the container.
The raft is capable of withstanding a drop into the water from its stowage height, and of being boarded from the water.
A raft over 185 kg that is not launched by a davit must be stowed for float-free launching, or be movable to either side.

technicalNotes.heading: Servicing
bullets: Serviced at an approved station at intervals not exceeding 12 months. An extension to 17 months may be permitted in exceptional cases where the ship cannot reach a station — it is an exception, granted, not a routine.
The HRU is a separate item with its own expiry: most disposable units are replaced at intervals not exceeding two years, and the date is stamped on the unit, not on the raft.
Check that the raft returned from service is the one that left, that the certificate matches the serial number, and that the container bands are the correct breaking type.
Look at how the lashing is rigged: a raft lashed with the senhouse slip on the wrong side of the HRU cannot float free, and this is the most common serious finding of the whole LSA suite.

helpTextEn: The hydrostatic release unit for a liferaft. Disposable units are replaced at 24 months; serviceable units go to an approved station. Always read the expiry stamped on the unit.

technicalNotes.heading: What it does and how it fails
bullets: The hydrostatic release unit cuts or releases the liferaft's lashing at a depth of not more than 4 m, so that the raft floats free of a sinking ship.
It is in the lashing, not in the painter: the painter goes to the weak link, and the two do different jobs.
Most units are disposable with a marked expiry, commonly two years from manufacture or from fitting; some are serviceable. The date on the unit is what counts.
The single most common rigging error is leading the painter through the HRU's release, or lashing the raft so that cutting the strop still leaves the raft held by the cradle.

technicalNotes.heading: Checking it without dismantling anything
bullets: Read the expiry stamp and record it: a stainless-looking unit is not an in-date unit.
Follow the strop by hand from the cradle, through the release, to the slip: it must be one continuous run with nothing else holding the raft.
Check the painter is made fast to the weak link and the weak link to the ship — not the painter direct to the deck.
A unit that has been painted over is condemned: the release mechanism is not designed to work through paint.

technicalNotes.heading: What a marine evacuation system is
bullets: A chute or slide from an embarkation station to one or more inflatable liferafts, so that a large number of people can leave without climbing down a ladder.
Deployment time and the number the system passes per minute are part of its approval.
The system is stowed inflated-ready and deployed by its own release; the rafts are part of the system, not separate rafts.

MES is serviced at an approved station; SOLAS III/20.8.3 requires it to be deployed from the ship on a rotational basis at intervals to be agreed with the Administration, so that each system is deployed at intervals not exceeding six years.

helpTextEn: Pilot ladder and its rigging arrangement. Carried in the register because the deck officer inspects it on the same rounds, and because PSC looks at it alongside the LSA.
commonPscFindings: Steps discoloured, split or secured with shackles or knots
Ladder not certified or the certificate not on board
Man-ropes, lifebuoy with light and heaving line not at the point of access

technicalNotes.heading: Construction — the figures a PSC officer measures
bullets: Steps of hardwood or equivalent, in one piece, free of knots, with an efficient non-slip surface.
Step dimensions: not less than 400 mm long, 115 mm wide and 25 mm thick, excluding any non-slip device.
Steps equally spaced at not less than 310 mm and not more than 350 mm apart.
Side ropes: two pairs of uncovered manila or equivalent rope, not less than 18 mm in diameter on each side, continuous and with no joins below the top step.
Spreader steps at intervals to stop the ladder twisting; the lowest spreader is on the fifth step from the bottom.
Not more than two replacement steps secured by a method different from the original, and any replaced step is put back at the original spacing.

technicalNotes.heading: Rigging, and the 9-metre rule
bullets: A pilot ladder alone is used where the climb from the water to the point of access is not more than 9 m.
Above 9 m a combination arrangement is used: an accommodation ladder with a pilot ladder, rigged as SOLAS V/23 and IMO Res. A.1045(27) as amended require.
Man-ropes, where used, are 28 to 32 mm in diameter, of manila or equivalent, secured at deck level.
Shackles, knots and cable clamps in the side ropes are not permitted; the ladder is secured to strong points on deck, not to a rail.
A lifebuoy with a self-igniting light and a heaving line are kept ready at the point of access, and the area is lit at night.
A responsible officer attends the embarkation and there is two-way communication with the bridge.

helpTextEn: Plain lifebuoy. Must be capable of being cast loose rapidly and must not be permanently secured.
commonPscFindings: Lifebuoy not readily available — lashed, painted to the rail or stowed in a locker
Ship's name and port of registry missing or illegible
Retro-reflective tape missing or degraded

technicalNotes.heading: What a lifebuoy has to be
bullets: Outer diameter not more than 800 mm and inner diameter not less than 400 mm — a ring outside that range is not a SOLAS lifebuoy however new it looks.
Mass not less than 2.5 kg. The ones fitted with a self-activating smoke signal that releases from the bridge must be at least 4 kg, because the mass is what operates the quick release.
Supports 14.5 kg of iron in fresh water for 24 hours.
Buoyancy comes from inherently buoyant material — never from rushes, cork shavings, granulated cork or any loose filling, and never from an air compartment that has to be inflated.
Withstands a drop into the water from its stowage height, or 30 m, whichever is greater.
Resistant to deterioration by oil and oil products, and of a highly visible colour.

technicalNotes.heading: Markings and what an inspector looks for
bullets: Ship's name and port of registry in block capitals of Roman script.
Retro-reflective material fitted per IMO Res. A.658(16): four patches evenly spaced round the ring, on both faces.
The grab line is secured at four equidistant points forming four equal loops — not two, and not knotted round the ring.
Nothing is painted over: paint on a lifebuoy is the single most common way its retro-reflective tape and its markings get written up.

technicalNotes.heading: How many, and where
bullets: Cargo ships carry a number by length: 8 below 100 m, 10 from 100 to under 150 m, 12 from 150 to under 200 m, 14 at 200 m and above (SOLAS III/32.1).
They are distributed so as to be readily available on both sides of the ship, and as far as practicable on all open decks leading to the ship's side; at least one is near the stern.

At least one on each side carries a buoyant lifeline; at least half the total carry self-igniting lights; and not fewer than two of those also carry self-activating smoke signals and can be released quickly from the navigating bridge.
A lifebuoy with a line is never also fitted with a light and smoke — the line would foul the release.
Stowed so it can be rapidly cast loose: never permanently secured, never lashed, never behind a lashed cover.

helpTextEn: Lifebuoy fitted with a self-igniting light. Record the light's battery expiry — it is the date that most often runs out unnoticed.
commonPscFindings: Lifebuoy not readily available — lashed, painted to the rail or stowed in a locker

technicalNotes.heading: What the light has to do
bullets: Burns with a luminous intensity of not less than 2 cd in all directions of the upper hemisphere.
Carries a source of energy for at least two hours.
Is not extinguished by water, and cannot be extinguished by the wind.
Flashing types flash at not less than 50 and not more than 70 flashes per minute, with the same effective luminous intensity.
Withstands the drop test with the lifebuoy from its stowage height or 30 m, whichever is greater.

technicalNotes.heading: The check that actually finds faults
bullets: Battery expiry date: read it, do not assume it. An in-date battery with green corrosion round the contacts is a failed light.
Test the water-activated contact by wetting it, not by pressing a test button that some makers do not fit.
The light is secured to the lifebuoy by its own lanyard, short enough that it cannot float away and long enough not to hold the ring on its edge.
Half the ship's lifebuoys must carry a light: count them against the certificate, because the count is what gets written up, not the condition.

technicalNotes.heading: What the smoke signal has to do
bullets: Emits smoke of a highly visible colour at a uniform rate for at least 15 minutes when floating in calm water.
Does not ignite or explode in an explosive atmosphere — which is why it is the signal used on a tanker's deck.
Does not swamp in a seaway, and keeps emitting when submerged in water for 10 seconds.
Expiry date is marked; it is a pyrotechnic and it expires like one.

technicalNotes.heading: Quick release from the bridge
bullets: At least two lifebuoys with both light and smoke must be capable of quick release from the navigating bridge.
The release is tested by operating it — a visual check of the pin proves nothing about the pelican hook underneath.
The lifebuoy on that release must be at least 4 kg: a lighter ring will not pull the smoke signal's actuating lanyard.
Expired smoke signals are landed as pyrotechnic waste, not thrown over the side and not kept 'for drills'.

technicalNotes.heading: Performance the jacket has to meet
bullets: Turns the mouth of an exhausted or unconscious wearer clear of the water in not more than 5 seconds.
Holds the mouth not less than 120 mm clear of the water, with the body inclined backwards at not less than 20 degrees from the vertical.
The wearer can jump from a height of at least 4.5 m into the water without injury and without dislodging or damaging the jacket.
Buoyancy is not reduced by more than 5% after 24 hours' immersion in fresh water.
Can be donned correctly within one minute without assistance, after a single demonstration — which is what makes the donning demonstration part of the drill and not a formality.
An adult jacket is for persons of 43 kg and above; below that the child and infant sizes apply.

technicalNotes.heading: What has to be attached to it
bullets: A whistle, firmly secured by a cord.
A light of not less than 0.75 cd in all directions of the upper hemisphere, burning for at least 8 hours; a flashing light does 50 to 70 flashes per minute.
Retro-reflective material to IMO Res. A.658(16).
Donning instructions, and the ship's name where the flag requires it.

technicalNotes.heading: Counting and stowing them

technicalNotes.heading: Why an inflatable is different
bullets: It has at least two separate compartments, inflates automatically on immersion, has a manual pull, and can be inflated by mouth.
It meets the same turning, freeboard and jump requirements as a solid jacket once inflated.
It is the only lifejacket type SOLAS requires to be serviced annually at an approved servicing station (SOLAS III/20.8.2).

technicalNotes.heading: The parts that fail
bullets: The gas cylinder: check it is full by mass against the figure stamped on it, and that it is screwed fully home. A finger-tight cylinder is the classic failure.
The automatic cartridge (bobbin or hydrostatic): it has an expiry date, and a bobbin that has been damp will have fired or will fire in the locker.
The green indicator on the firing head — red means it has fired or is not armed.
The oral inflation tube's non-return valve, and the seams: an annual service includes an overnight air-holding test.

technicalNotes.heading: Performance the suit has to meet
bullets: Can be unpacked and donned without assistance within 2 minutes, including any associated clothing and a lifejacket if the suit needs one.
Covers the whole body except the face; hands are covered unless permanently attached gloves are provided.
The wearer can climb up and down a vertical ladder of at least 5 m, jump from a height of at least 4.5 m without damaging the suit, swim a short distance, and board a survival craft.
Limits the fall in body core temperature to not more than 2°C after 6 hours' immersion in calm water of 0 to 2°C.
A suit not inherently buoyant is worn with a lifejacket; the stowage must hold both.

technicalNotes.heading: The air-pressure test — the one that finds the real defects
bullets: MSC.1/Circ.1047 and MSC.1/Circ.1114 set out the air-pressure (leak) test: the suit is sealed, inflated to a low pressure and checked for leaks, typically by immersion or by soap solution on the seams.
Common guidance is a test at intervals not exceeding three years, and annually once the suit is more than ten years old — confirm the interval against the flag's instruction and the maker's manual.
Zip condition is the usual failure: a stiff, corroded or ungreased zip will not close in the two minutes the officer has.
Wax or the maker's zip lubricant, not grease or oil, which attacks the zip's tape.
Check the seals at face, wrists and ankles for perishing, and the retro-reflective tape and light.

technicalNotes.heading: How many and where
bullets: One for every person on board, stowed at the muster station or at the person's cabin as the ship's arrangement provides.
Ships operating in cold water carry them for everyone; the count and stowage are on the Safety Equipment Certificate's record of equipment.
A suit stowed in a bag that has been sat on for a year will have a set crease in the visor area — open and repack them at the annual inspection.

technicalNotes.heading: What it is and how it is found
bullets: A 406 MHz beacon registered to the ship, whose alert reaches a rescue co-ordination centre via satellite, carrying the ship's identity.
The 121.5 MHz element is for homing on scene, not for alerting.
Float-free EPIRBs are released by their own hydrostatic release unit, which has its own expiry date — commonly two years, marked on the unit.
Registration must be current: a beacon registered to a previous owner sends rescuers to the wrong ship.

technicalNotes.heading: The tests and the dates
bullets: Monthly: the self-test, using the beacon's own test function — never by letting it transmit a real alert.
Annual: the test required by SOLAS IV/15.9, checking the beacon for its capability to operate properly, including the frequency, the coded identification and the battery.
Five-yearly: shore-based maintenance at an approved facility.
Battery expiry and HRU expiry are separate dates and are both recorded; an in-date battery on an expired HRU is still a finding.
If it is ever activated by accident, tell the RCC immediately — an unreported false alert is a far bigger problem than the mistake.

helpTextEn: Search-and-rescue transponder carried on the bridge for transfer to the survival craft.
commonPscFindings: Battery expired

technicalNotes.heading: How a SART shows on a radar
bullets: A 9 GHz radar SART responds to an X-band radar and paints a line of twelve blips extending outward from its position along the bearing.
As the searching ship closes, the blips become arcs and then concentric circles: that change is the range cue, and it is how you know you are close.
It does not respond to an S-band (3 GHz) radar — searching on S-band alone will find nothing.
Detection range is roughly 5 nautical miles from a ship's radar antenna at 15 m, and around 30 nautical miles from an aircraft at 3,000 ft.
An AIS-SART instead transmits AIS position reports and appears as an AIS target, not as a radar pattern.

technicalNotes.heading: Checks
bullets: Monthly: the self-test as the maker describes, and confirm the visual/audible indication.
Do not test by radar interrogation without informing others — it puts a distress pattern on every screen in range.
Battery expiry date, and the mounting bracket: a SART that cannot be got out of its bracket with cold hands is no use.
Stowed so it can be rapidly placed in a survival craft, and its position marked.

helpTextEn: One record per portable extinguisher. technicalNotes.heading: Size, and how many
bullets: A portable extinguisher has a total mass of not more than 23 kg fully charged; anything heavier is a wheeled unit and is counted separately.
Minimum charges: 5 kg for dry powder, 5 kg for CO2, and 9 litres for a fluid (foam or water) extinguisher.
Accommodation, service spaces and control stations carry not fewer than five portable extinguishers in total.
At least one extinguisher intended for use in a space is stowed near the entrance to that space — an extinguisher deep inside a burning space is not an extinguisher.

CO2 extinguishers are not placed in accommodation spaces. Where they are in control stations or spaces with electrical equipment, their capacity is limited so that the CO2 could not raise the concentration above 5% of the gross volume of the space.

technicalNotes.heading: Spare charges
bullets: Spare charges are provided for 100% of the first ten extinguishers and 50% of the remainder capable of being recharged on board, up to a maximum of 60 in total.
For extinguishers that cannot be recharged on board, additional portable extinguishers of the same type, capacity and number are carried instead of spare charges.
Instructions for recharging are carried on board.
A ship that keeps its spares locked in a store on the other side of the ship from the extinguishers has met the letter and missed the point.

technicalNotes.heading: Testing and the dates that matter
bullets: Monthly: a visual check that each extinguisher is in place, unobstructed, the pressure gauge (where fitted) is in the green, the pin and seal are intact, and the hose is not perished.
Annual: examine every extinguisher against MSC.1/Circ.1432; weigh CO2 extinguishers and recharge any that have lost more than 10% of the charge mass.

Internal examination and a discharge test at the interval in the maintenance plan — commonly five years — and a hydraulic pressure test of the cylinder at the longer interval the maker and the plan set, commonly ten years for CO2.
One extinguisher of each type is discharged by the crew each year as part of the training under SOLAS II-2/15, which is also how the crew finds out how short a discharge really is.
Read the classes on the label. Dry powder on a live switchboard is not the same decision as CO2, and foam on a live electrical fire is not a decision at all.

helpTextEn: Fire hydrant on the fire main. Record the pressure observed at the most remote hydrant when the fire pumps are tested — that is the figure a surveyor asks for.

technicalNotes.heading: Pressure and placement
bullets: Hydrants are placed so that two jets of water, not emanating from the same hydrant, can reach any part of the ship normally accessible while at sea — one of them from a single length of hose.
At least one of the two jets can reach any part of any cargo space when empty, any ro-ro space and any vehicle space.

Minimum pressure at the two hydrants, with the required pumps running: 0.27 N/mm² for cargo ships of 6,000 gross tonnage and above, and 0.25 N/mm² below that. Passenger ships are higher and graded by tonnage.
The valve is arranged so that a hose can be removed while the fire pumps are running: every hydrant has an isolating valve, and it must actually turn.
Hydrants in exposed positions are protected against frost where the ship trades cold.

technicalNotes.heading: The joint the whole system stands on
bullets: The hose coupling is the ship's weakest link when help arrives from outside: a ship whose hoses will not mate with the terminal's is a ship fighting alone.

Common patterns you will meet: **Storz** — symmetrical (hermaphrodite) lug coupling, quarter-turn, no male or female half, standard across most of continental Europe and widely used at sea; **instantaneous** — British pattern with a male tail and a spring-latched female; **NH / NST** — American threaded, male and female; **Guillemin** — French, lug and cam; **Nakajima** — Japanese, lug type.

Storz sizes are lettered by nominal bore, commonly A (about 110 mm), B (about 75 mm), C (about 52 mm) and D (about 25 mm). A Storz B will not mate with a Storz C, and adapters between the sizes are what a well-found ship keeps in the fire locker.
Because a symmetrical coupling has no male half, two ships with Storz can always be joined; two ships with different threaded patterns cannot without an adapter.

This is exactly why the **international shore connection** exists: it is one standard flange, carried by every ship, that lets shore fire-fighting water into the ship's fire main whatever the local coupling is.
Keep the gaskets. A coupling with a perished or missing gasket passes a visual check and fails under pressure.

technicalNotes.heading: Checks that find real defects
bullets: Open every hydrant valve at least once in the maintenance cycle: a valve that has not been turned in three years is seized, and it is seized when you need it.
Blank caps present, on their chains, and free — a cap that has to be hammered off is a lost minute.
Corrosion at the valve spindle and at the flange; wastage in the branch pipe behind the hydrant, which is where the fire main actually fails.
Isolating valves for the section: located, labelled, and free to operate.

technicalNotes.heading: Length, and how many
bullets: Machinery spaces: hoses of 10 to 15 m.
Other spaces and open decks: 15 to 20 m.
Open decks of a ship of more than 30 m breadth: up to 25 m.
Number on a cargo ship: one for each 30 m of ship's length, plus one spare, and never fewer than five in total — excluding any hose required in the machinery space.
Each hose has a nozzle and the necessary couplings and is kept with its hydrant, not in a store.
In accommodation, service and machinery spaces hoses may be kept connected to the hydrants at all times.

technicalNotes.heading: Nozzles
bullets: Standard nozzle sizes are 12, 16 and 19 mm, or as near as possible.
Accommodation and service spaces: no nozzle larger than 12 mm is needed.
Machinery spaces and exterior locations: 19 mm, or the nearest size, to give the greatest discharge from the smallest pump.
All nozzles are dual-purpose — jet and spray — and have a shutoff. Spray is what protects the man behind it; jet is what reaches.

technicalNotes.heading: Testing and storage
bullets: MSC.1/Circ.1432 requires all hoses, nozzles, couplings and hydrants to be inspected annually.

Pressure testing is at the interval in the ship's maintenance plan and after any repair; hoses are tested to the maximum fire main pressure. Check the plan and the flag's instruction rather than assuming an interval.
Store them dry and rolled or flaked as the box allows. A hose stowed wet rots from the inside and passes every visual check until it bursts.
Mark each hose with its station. A hose that lives at hydrant 12 and is found at hydrant 3 is a hose that was borrowed and not returned.

technicalNotes.heading: The standard dimensions — worth knowing by heart
bullets: Outside diameter of the flange: 178 mm.
Inside diameter: 64 mm.
Bolt circle diameter: 132 mm.
Four holes of 19 mm diameter, equidistant on the bolt circle, slotted out to the flange periphery so the flange can be fitted without withdrawing the bolts.
Flange thickness: 14.5 mm minimum.
Four bolts of 16 mm diameter and 50 mm length, with eight washers and a gasket.
The flange face is flat on one side and fitted with a coupling to suit the ship's hydrants on the other.

technicalNotes.heading: What it is for, and where it lives
bullets: It lets a shore fire-fighting main, or another ship, feed the ship's fire main through one internationally standard joint, whatever coupling pattern the two sides normally use.
Cargo ships of 500 gross tonnage and above carry at least one; the ship must be able to use it on either side.
The connection is kept with its bolts, nuts, washers and gasket, in one place, accessible from either side of the ship, and its position is marked on the fire control plan.
The complete set is the requirement: a flange found without its gasket and bolts is the same finding as no flange at all.
Made of material suitable for 1.0 N/mm² service, with a gasket to match.

bullets: Capacity not less than 40% of the total capacity of the fire pumps required, and in any case not less than 25 m³/h.
Capable of delivering two jets of water at the required pressure.
Located outside the space containing the main fire pumps, with its own sea suction, so a fire in the machinery space cannot take both.

technicalNotes.heading: Fuel and the weekly test
bullets: Fuel in the service tank sufficient for at least three hours at full load, with reserves outside the main machinery space for a further fifteen hours.
Weekly: start the pump, run it, and prove it delivers pressure at a hydrant — starting it and stopping it at the pump proves only that it turns.
Prime the suction and check the sea valve is free: a seized emergency sea suction valve is the failure that makes the whole pump irrelevant.
Record the running hours and the starting method used; a pump that only ever starts on the electric starter has an untested hand start.

technicalNotes.heading: The sample that matters
bullets: Foam concentrate is sampled and analysed periodically at a competent laboratory — commonly annually after three years from manufacture, per MSC.1/Circ.1312 and MSC.1/Circ.1432; confirm against the ship's plan and the maker.
The test looks for sediment, pH, viscosity, expansion ratio and drainage time.
Degraded concentrate is replaced, never topped up with a different brand or type: mixing types can destroy the performance of both.
Keep the certificate of analysis with the ship's records; the certificate, not the tank level, is what proves the foam works.

technicalNotes.heading: Practical care
bullets: Tank level, and the tank's coating: many concentrates attack ordinary steel.
Keep the tank sealed. Evaporation and contamination both change the concentration, and it is the concentration that sets the application rate.
Note the type — protein, fluoroprotein, AFFF, alcohol-resistant — on the tank and in the plan. The wrong type on a polar solvent cargo does nothing.
Environmental rules on fluorinated foams are changing; when a foam is replaced, check what the ship's next trading area accepts.

bullets: Machinery spaces: the quantity of CO2 is the greater of 40% of the gross volume of the largest machinery space excluding the casing, or 35% of that volume including the casing.
Cargo spaces: 30% of the gross volume of the largest cargo space to be protected.
For machinery spaces, 85% of the gas is discharged within two minutes.

Two separate controls are required: one for opening the valve of the piping into the space, and one for discharging the gas from the containers. Both are in a release box that gives a clear warning when opened.

technicalNotes.heading: The interlocks and alarms
bullets: An audible and visual alarm sounds in the protected space before the gas is released, with a delay long enough for people to get out.
The alarm is distinct from every other alarm on board — that is the point of it.
Ventilation stops and closures operate; the fuel supply shuts; the space is sealed before release.
The means of release is in a position readily accessible outside the protected space, unlikely to be cut off by a fire in it.

technicalNotes.heading: Servicing intervals to know
bullets: Annual: check the cylinders' contents by weight or by level, examine the release lines, alarms, and the door interlocks, and check the pilot cylinders.
Every two years: blow through the distribution piping with dry air to prove it is clear, and check the release lines for leaks.
Ten-yearly: hydrostatic testing of a sample of the cylinders, commonly 10%, per the maintenance plan and MSC.1/Circ.1432.
A cylinder that has lost more than the allowed percentage of its charge is refilled or replaced — the whole system is designed on the total mass.
Never enter a CO2 room without treating it as an enclosed space: a leaking cylinder makes it one.

Deck seal or non-return valve defective

technicalNotes.heading: The two numbers
bullets: The gas delivered by the system contains not more than 5% oxygen by volume.
Cargo tanks are kept at not more than 8% oxygen by volume, and at a positive pressure at all times.
The system is capable of delivering at least 125% of the maximum discharge rate of the cargo pumps.
Below those figures the tank is not inerted, whatever the plant is doing.

technicalNotes.heading: The parts that protect the ship
bullets: The deck water seal: the non-return barrier that stops cargo gas from backing up into the machinery space. Its water level and its low-level alarm are checked daily in service.
The non-return valve on deck, in series with the water seal.
The P/V breaker (liquid-filled), which is the last protection against over- and under-pressure. Its liquid level and freezing point matter in cold weather.
Scrubber, blowers, deck isolating valve, and the oxygen analyser — which is only as good as its last calibration.
Alarms and trips to check: high oxygen content, low gas pressure, high gas temperature, low water in the seal, blower failure.
Purging before gas-freeing is done so that the tank atmosphere passes out of the flammable range rather than through it.

attributeSchema.labelEn: Fuel / power shut-off operates on release

helpTextEn: Galley range hood extinguishing system, its duct and its fuel/power shut-off.
commonPscFindings: Grease build-up in the hood and duct
Manual release obstructed by galley equipment
Service overdue; nozzle caps missing
Fuel or power shut-off does not operate on release

helpTextEn: Local application system protecting main engine, purifiers, boiler burners and other high-risk machinery items.
commonPscFindings: Nozzles displaced by maintenance work and no longer aimed at the risk
Detection heads dirty or bypassed
System left isolated after maintenance

helpTextEn: Smoke detector head. Record the loop and address so the monthly sample test can be rotated through the installation.
commonPscFindings: Detectors painted over, taped up or removed during works
Monthly sample test not recorded; five-yearly full test overdue
Faults standing at the panel and not rectified
No spare detector heads or test equipment on board

technicalNotes.heading: Sensitivity and spacing
bullets: Smoke detectors operate before the smoke density exceeds 12.5% obscuration per metre, and not below 2% obscuration per metre.
Spacing: not more than 11 m apart and not more than 5.5 m from a bulkhead, covering not more than 74 m² of deck area each.
Detectors are positioned clear of beams and of ventilation inlets and outlets, which is where a badly sited head sits and never sees smoke.
Every detector is tested for correct operation by producing hot air, smoke or aerosol particles within the appropriate range of sensitivity, and is then restored to normal.

technicalNotes.heading: Common faults
bullets: Dust and paint: a painted-over detector head is a dead detector, and it is the most common finding after any refit.
A detector removed for work and never refitted, with its base capped: the panel shows no fault and the space has no cover.
Zone labelling at the panel that no longer matches the compartment names after a conversion.
Test heads on a rotation so that every detector on board is tested inside the maintenance cycle, and record which ones — 'panel tested' is not a record.

helpTextEn: Heat detector head, typically in the galley and machinery spaces.
commonPscFindings: Detectors painted over, taped up or removed during works
Monthly sample test not recorded; five-yearly full test overdue
Faults standing at the panel and not rectified
No spare detector heads or test equipment on board

technicalNotes.heading: Operating temperature and spacing
bullets: Heat detectors operate before the temperature exceeds 78°C, and not before it reaches 54°C, when the temperature rises to those limits at a rate of less than 1°C per minute.
At higher rates of rise the detector operates within temperature limits appropriate to avoid spurious operation.
Spacing: not more than 9 m apart and not more than 4.5 m from a bulkhead, covering not more than 37 m² of deck area each.
In drying rooms, galleys and similar spaces the operating temperature may be raised to suit — but only where the Administration permits it, and not above the limit set.

helpTextEn: Flame (IR/UV) detector, typically over boiler fronts and purifier flats.

helpTextEn: The fire detection and alarm panel on the bridge, with its repeaters. Standing disablements are the finding surveyors and PSC officers look for first.
commonPscFindings: Zones or loops isolated and left isolated
Standing faults not entered in the defect log
Standby batteries flat or beyond their life

technicalNotes.heading: What the panel has to do
bullets: Indicate the section in which a detector or manual call point has operated, both visually and audibly, at the panel and at a position where it will be immediately received by a responsible member of the crew.
Power supply from two sources, one of which is an emergency source, with automatic changeover.
A fault in the loop must not disable the whole system, and must itself be indicated as a fault distinct from a fire alarm.
The panel is tested at intervals with a means for functionally testing and restoring the detectors to normal.

technicalNotes.heading: Working with it honestly
bullets: Isolated zones: keep a written record of every isolation, why, and by whom. An isolation that outlives the work it was for is how ships burn.
A standing fault that everyone has learned to ignore is a fault, and it will be the first thing an inspector points at.
Confirm the repeater panels — bridge, ECR, fire station — all show the same state.
After any hot work, confirm the zone was restored and record the time.

helpTextEn: Fire alarm sounder or bell, and the flashing beacons in high-noise spaces.
commonPscFindings: Sounder inaudible over machinery noise
Sounder painted over or disconnected

commonPscFindings: Calibration overdue or the calibration gas expired
Sampling lines blocked

helpTextEn: Portable multi-gas meter used for enclosed space entry and hot work. Bump test before each use, calibrate at the maker's interval.
commonPscFindings: Calibration overdue or the calibration gas expired
No bump test records
Aspirator hose perished or the probe missing
Insufficient meters for the enclosed-entry procedure

technicalNotes.heading: The right instrument for the hazard
bullets: A catalytic (pellistor) LFL meter needs oxygen to work and gives a false low reading in an inert atmosphere — it must not be used to clear an inerted tank.
In an inerted or oxygen-deficient tank, use a tankscope or an equivalent instrument that reads hydrocarbon by volume rather than by combustion.
Oxygen, hydrocarbon, hydrogen sulphide and benzene are four separate measurements. One reading clears one hazard, not the space.
Personal H2S monitors are worn where the cargo or the terminal requires it, and their alarms are not silenced.

technicalNotes.heading: Making a reading mean something
bullets: Bump-test before use with the test gas; calibrate on the maker's schedule. Record both — an uncalibrated instrument produces a number, not evidence.
Check the sample line and probe for length, condition and blockage; a cracked line reads fresh air all the way down the tank.
Take readings at several levels: heavier-than-air vapours collect low, and a reading at the hatch clears nothing.
Allow the full response time for the length of hose being used before you believe the number.

attributeSchema.labelEn: Pressure at or above the maker's minimum

helpTextEn: Self-contained breathing apparatus set. Cylinder pressure is checked weekly and verified by the responsible officer monthly; the cylinder is hydrostatically tested every 5 years.
commonPscFindings: Cylinder pressure below the maker's minimum
Cylinder hydrostatic test date expired
Face mask seal perished; no spare cylinders charged
Set stowed in a locked space or not with the fireman's outfit

technicalNotes.heading: What the set has to be
bullets: A self-contained compressed-air breathing apparatus with a cylinder of at least 1,200 litres of free air, or capable of at least 30 minutes' duration.
Full face mask, positive-pressure demand valve, harness and a low-pressure warning device.
The warning whistle sounds while about a quarter of the air remains — typically around 50 to 55 bar on a 200 bar set. That is your margin to get out, not your margin to keep working.
Working pressures are commonly 200 or 300 bar; a 300 bar cylinder in a 200 bar charging line is a mistake that only shows up when you need the duration.
Cylinders may be steel or composite. Composite cylinders have a finite service life stamped on them — typically 15 years — after which they are withdrawn regardless of condition.

technicalNotes.heading: Spare charges and the compressor
bullets: Two spare charges are provided for each required breathing apparatus.
A ship fitted with means to fully recharge the air cylinders free of contamination on board may carry one spare charge per apparatus instead.
Tankers, and ships carrying more than a stated number of sets, follow the same rule with the higher number of outfits required by SOLAS II-2/10.10.
Where the ship has a compressor, the air quality is what makes it legal: filters changed on the maker's schedule, and an air-quality test at the interval in the maintenance plan.

technicalNotes.heading: The monthly check that is worth doing properly
bullets: Cylinder pressure: not less than 80% of the full charge. Below that, recharge — do not sign it as serviceable.
High-pressure leak test: open the cylinder valve, close it, and watch the gauge. A drop of more than about 10 bar in a minute is a leak to be found.
Whistle test: vent slowly and confirm the whistle sounds at the correct pressure, and keeps sounding.
Positive pressure: don the mask, breathe, then break the face seal with a finger — you should feel air flowing outward.
Face seal test: block the inlet and inhale; the mask should collapse onto the face and hold.
Harness, straps and buckles, the mask's visor for crazing, and the rubber for perishing. A mask stored in sunlight is a mask with a limited life.
Beard growth breaks the face seal. This is not a rule about appearance; it is the reason a fit test fails.

technicalNotes.heading: Cylinder testing
bullets: Hydrostatic (or, where permitted, ultrasonic) testing of the cylinder at the interval stamped on it and required by the standard it was made to — commonly five years.
The test date is stamped on the cylinder shoulder together with the standard, the working pressure and the test pressure. Read the stamps rather than the paperwork.
An out-of-test cylinder is unusable, full or not, and a charging station ashore will refuse it.
Keep a register: cylinder serial, standard, working pressure, last test, next test. Sets get swapped between stations and the register is what keeps the dates with the metal.

helpTextEn: Emergency escape breathing device. EEBDs are for escape only, never for fire fighting or enclosed space entry — that statement belongs on the training record too.
commonPscFindings: Pressure indicator outside the green band
Unit expired or the hydrostatic test overdue
EEBD stowed behind stores or its position not marked
Fewer units than the number shown on the fire control plan
Training units mixed in with the service units

technicalNotes.heading: What an EEBD is, and what it is not
bullets: An emergency escape breathing device provides air or oxygen to escape from a space with a dangerous atmosphere. Service duration is at least 10 minutes.
It is **not** for fighting a fire, and **not** for entering a space. Using an EEBD to go back in is the misuse the regulation is written against.
It has a hood covering the whole head, or a full face piece, giving protection to the eyes, nose and mouth.
Marked with brief instructions or diagrams, clearly illustrating its use, and the marking is visible where it is stowed.

technicalNotes.heading: How many, and the checks
bullets: At least two in the accommodation spaces, and additional units in machinery spaces as SOLAS II-2/13 requires, positioned so as to be readily accessible from the escape routes.
Training units are provided separately and are clearly marked as training units — a training unit found in a service position is a serious finding.
Monthly: check the pressure indicator, the seal, the case for damage, and that the stowage position is marked and unobstructed.
Service at the interval the maker sets; most units have both a service interval and an overall life.
A unit whose seal is broken is out of service until it has been checked, regardless of what the gauge shows.

attributeSchema.labelEn: Protective clothing, boots and gloves complete
attributeSchema.labelTr: Koruyucu giysi, çizme ve eldiven tam

attributeSchema.labelEn: Helmet undamaged and within its life

attributeSchema.labelTr: Yangına dayanıklı can halatı mevcut ve sağlam

helpTextEn: Complete fireman's outfit — protective clothing, boots, gloves, helmet, safety lamp, axe, lifeline and breathing apparatus. Record the SCBA set as a child of this outfit so the two stay together.
commonPscFindings: Outfit incomplete — lamp, axe or lifeline missing
Protective clothing damaged, contaminated or beyond its life
Outfits not stowed widely separated as required
Locker locked and the key not readily available

technicalNotes.heading: What makes up one outfit
bullets: Protective clothing of material to protect the skin from the heat radiating from the fire and from burns and scalding by steam, with an outer surface that is water-resistant.
Boots of rubber or other electrically non-conducting material, and gloves of the same protection.
A rigid helmet giving effective protection against impact.
An electric safety lamp (hand lantern) with a burning period of at least three hours; on tankers and in hazardous spaces it is of an approved explosion-proof type.
An axe with a handle provided with high-voltage insulation.
A self-contained breathing apparatus meeting the FSS Code.

technicalNotes.heading: The lifeline, and the test people forget
bullets: A fireproof lifeline of at least 30 m in length is carried with each breathing apparatus.
It is tested by suspending a load of 3.2 kN for five minutes without failure.
The line's snap hook and belt harness are part of the tested item.
Do the test and record it: it is one of the few LSA/FFE tests that can be done on board with a known weight, and it is one of the most commonly missing records.

technicalNotes.heading: How many outfits
bullets: Cargo ships carry at least two fireman's outfits.
Tankers carry at least four (SOLAS II-2/10.10).
Ships carrying dangerous goods carry additional outfits and equipment as SOLAS II-2/19 requires.
Outfits are stored in widely separated positions, so that one fire cannot deny the crew all of them, and their positions are on the fire control plan.

commonPscFindings: Lifeline missing from the outfit

helpTextEn: Fireman's axe with an insulated handle, part of the outfit.

helpTextEn: Two-way portable explosion-protected radios for the fire party.
commonPscFindings: Fewer radios than required
Batteries flat or the charger inoperative
Radios not of an explosion-protected type where required

attributeSchema.labelEn: Not wedged, hooked or tied open
Seals, hinges and closer in good order

helpTextEn: Fire door in an A- or B-class division. The single most common PSC finding on structural fire protection is a self-closing door held open with a hook, a wedge or a cargo lashing.
commonPscFindings: Self-closing door wedged, hooked or tied open
Door does not close fully or latch
Remote release from the bridge inoperative
Door seal, hinge or closer defective; holes cut for cables
Door not marked with its class or the sign painted over

technicalNotes.heading: A-class and B-class, and what they mean
bullets: A-class divisions are steel, insulated so the unexposed side does not rise more than the stated amount in 60 minutes (A-60), 30 minutes (A-30), 15 (A-15) or 0 (A-0), and prevent the passage of smoke and flame for one hour in the standard fire test.
B-class divisions prevent the passage of flame for the first half hour, with insulation ratings B-15 and B-0.
The door carries the same rating as the division it is in; a fire door held open by a wedge is a hole in that division.
Self-closing doors close against an inclination of 3.5 degrees opposing closure.

technicalNotes.heading: Hold-back arrangements
bullets: Where a fire door is held open, the release is remote and fails safe: loss of power closes the door.
The release is operable from the navigation bridge and from at the door.
Test both, and test that the door then closes fully and latches — a door that closes to within an inch of the frame has failed.
Check the intumescent strip and the closing sequence on double doors.

attributeSchema.labelEn: Position indicator agrees with the blade
Local and remote controls accessible and marked
attributeSchema.labelTr: Yerel ve uzaktan kumandalar erişilebilir ve işaretli

helpTextEn: Fire damper in a ventilation duct. Test the damper itself, not just the handle — a linkage that moves while the blade stays open is a classic finding.
commonPscFindings: Damper seized or the linkage disconnected from the blade
Position indicator wrong
Damper not identified or not shown on the fire control plan
Control painted over or inaccessible behind lagging

technicalNotes.heading: What is being tested
bullets: The damper closes fully, from the remote control position and locally, and stays closed.
Every damper is marked with the space it serves, and the marking matches the fire control plan.
Remote closing arrangements are tested at the interval in the maintenance plan; a damper that has not been closed in years will be seized by paint.
The blade's edge seal and the spindle gland: a damper that closes but does not seal has done nothing.
Ventilation to a machinery space is arranged to be stopped and the openings closed from outside the space.

attributeSchema.labelEn: Can be closed from outside the space

helpTextEn: Closing appliances for ventilation openings — flaps, dampers and skylights serving machinery and cargo spaces, operable from outside the space.
commonPscFindings: Closing device seized with paint or corrosion
Cannot be operated from outside the space
Position of the control not marked

attributeSchema.labelEn: Stops all fans serving the space

helpTextEn: Remote stops for the ventilation fans serving machinery and cargo spaces, grouped outside the space they serve.
commonPscFindings: Remote stop does not stop every fan serving the space
Controls not grouped or not marked
Stop tested only at the panel and never proved at the fan

technicalNotes.heading: Stopping the air to a fire
bullets: The ventilation serving machinery spaces, cargo spaces, vehicle spaces and accommodation can be stopped from outside the space it serves.
The stops are grouped and clearly marked, in a position that will not be cut off by the fire.
Stopping the fans and closing the dampers are two different actions, and a fixed gas system needs both.
Test the stops from the actual control position — proving the fan stops from the ECR does not prove the emergency stop works.

attributeSchema.labelEn: Reset and re-set after the test

attributeSchema.labelTr: Uzaktan kumanda istasyonu işaretli ve erişilebilir

helpTextEn: Quick-closing valve on a fuel oil, lubricating oil or other flammable oil tank, operable from outside the space. Always confirm the valve is re-set after the test.
commonPscFindings: Valve seized, or the wire and pulleys corroded
Valve left tripped or not re-set after the test
Remote station obstructed or not marked
Test not recorded in the maintenance plan

technicalNotes.heading: The valve that stops a machinery-space fire feeding itself
bullets: Every fuel oil, lubricating oil and other flammable oil tank with an outlet below the top has a valve capable of being closed from a safe position outside the space.
The remote closing is normally by pull-wire, hydraulic or pneumatic release, arranged so that loss of the medium closes the valve.
The release position is outside the space it protects, marked, and unobstructed.
It is tested by operating the remote release and confirming the valve has actually shut — pulling the wire and hearing a click proves nothing.

technicalNotes.heading: Why they fail
bullets: The valve is reset after the test and then left in a half-cocked position that will not close on demand.
Pull-wires seize in their conduits, or are painted into them.
The release box is behind stores, or its door is locked and the key is in the ECR.
Test them on a rotation so that every valve is proved within the maintenance cycle, and log which ones.

helpTextEn: Emergency generator. Carried in this register because the emergency source of power feeds the emergency fire pump, the alarm systems and the emergency lighting, and is demonstrated at the Safety Equipment survey.
commonPscFindings: Will not auto-start on blackout within the required time
Independent fuel tank low or the supply valve shut
Starting batteries flat; charger inoperative
Space used for stowage; access obstructed
Run-on-load record not maintained

technicalNotes.heading: What it has to do, and how fast
bullets: Supplies the emergency services automatically within 45 seconds of the failure of the main source of electrical power.
Fuel for at least 18 hours on a cargo ship, and 36 hours on a passenger ship.
Located above the uppermost continuous deck, outside the machinery casing, and reachable from the open deck.
Starts in cold condition at 0°C; where that is impracticable, or where lower temperatures are expected, heating is provided.
Three consecutive starts from the stored energy, with a second independent source unless a hand start is provided.

technicalNotes.heading: The weekly test, done properly
bullets: Run it on load, not off load. A generator that runs happily with no load can still fail to take the switchboard.
Prove the automatic start by simulating a blackout where the ship's procedures allow it — the changeover is the thing being tested, not the engine.
Check the starting batteries' electrolyte and charge, the air bottle pressure where fitted, and the fuel level against the 18-hour figure.
Emergency lighting, steering, fire pump, and the radio installation are the loads that matter; walk the ship and confirm they come up.
Log the run: date, duration, load, and what was proved.

helpTextEn: Emergency switchboard and its changeover arrangement.
commonPscFindings: Changeover not tested or the record not maintained
Insulating matting missing or damaged
Space used for stowage

attributeSchema.labelTr: Kutup başları temiz, gresli ve sıkı

helpTextEn: Emergency and transitional source of power batteries.
commonPscFindings: Battery beyond its service life or failing the discharge test
Terminals corroded; ventilation blocked
Battery room used for stowage or naked lights permitted

technicalNotes.heading: The transitional source
bullets: Where the emergency generator takes time to come on load, an accumulator battery supplies the transitional source of emergency power automatically and without interruption.
It supplies the emergency lighting, the navigation-critical systems and the alarms for the period SOLAS II-1 requires, typically 30 minutes.
The battery room is ventilated to atmosphere, and the ventilation is what stops hydrogen accumulating — check that the trunk is clear before believing the fan.
Terminals clean and greased, electrolyte level and specific gravity within limits, and the charger's float and boost settings correct.
No naked light, no smoking, no tools left across the terminals: a spanner bridging a battery bank is the classic engine-room accident.

attributeSchema.labelEn: Can be closed from outside the space

helpTextEn: Machinery space skylight and its closing arrangement, which must be closeable from outside the space before a fixed gas release.
commonPscFindings: Skylight seized open or the closing wire parted
Cannot be closed from outside the space
Glass cracked or the frame corroded

attributeSchema.labelEn: Last local and remote operation test
attributeSchema.labelTr: Son yerel ve uzaktan çalıştırma testi

attributeSchema.labelEn: Seals sound; door tight when closed

helpTextEn: Watertight door, tested locally and remotely and logged. Also relevant to damage control, so it appears on the damage control plan as well as the fire control plan.
commonPscFindings: Door will not close in the required time
Alarm inoperative or the local control obstructed
Door left open at sea contrary to the standing order
Seals damaged; door leaks when tested

technicalNotes.heading: Operation and drills
bullets: Power-operated watertight doors close from the bridge and locally from both sides.
Closing time is controlled — fast enough to be effective, slow enough to be survivable — with audible and visual warning during closure.
Local operation is possible with the power off, by hand, from both sides.
Doors are exercised at the interval SOLAS II-1 requires, and the drill covers closing them from the bridge as well as locally.

technicalNotes.heading: What is checked
bullets: Rubber seals for permanent set, cracking and missing sections; the sealing faces for paint build-up.

technicalNotes.heading: What has to be on it
bullets: The control stations, the fire sections enclosed by A-class divisions, the sections enclosed by B-class divisions, and the fire detection and alarm systems.

The sprinkler installation, the extinguishing appliances, the means of access to compartments and decks, and the ventilation system including fan control positions, damper positions and the identification numbers of the ventilating fans serving each section.
Symbols are those of IMO Res. A.952(23).
A booklet may be used in place of a plan, and a copy of it or the plan is kept ashore with the company.
The plan is kept permanently exhibited, and it is in the working language of the ship as well as English or French where the flag requires.

technicalNotes.heading: The outside container
bullets: A duplicate set of fire control plans, or a booklet, is permanently stored in a prominently marked weathertight enclosure **outside the deckhouse**, for the assistance of shore-side fire-fighting personnel.
The container is marked so a fire brigade arriving at night can find it: this is what it is for.
Check it holds the current revision — a plan updated on the bridge and not in the box is the usual finding.
Check it is weathertight and that the plans inside are dry and legible.

technicalNotes.heading: What the muster list must state
bullets: The details of the general emergency alarm and the public address system, and the action to be taken by crew and passengers when it is sounded.
How the order to abandon ship will be given.
The duties assigned to each member of the crew, including the closing of watertight doors, fire doors, valves, scuppers, side scuttles, skylights, portholes and similar openings.

The equipping of survival craft and the other life-saving appliances, the preparation and launching of survival craft, the general preparations of other life-saving appliances, the muster of passengers, and the use of communication equipment.
The duties assigned to crew in relation to passengers, and the substitutes for key persons who may become disabled.

technicalNotes.heading: Keeping it true
bullets: Prepared before the ship proceeds to sea, and updated whenever the crew changes — a muster list with last trip's names is not a muster list.
Exhibited in conspicuous places, including the bridge, the engine room and the crew accommodation.
The duties on it match the duties actually practised in the drill; if the drill has evolved, the list is amended, not the drill hidden.
Individual duty cards in the cabins match the list.

technicalNotes.heading: What the training manual covers
bullets: SOLAS III/35: a training manual is provided in each crew mess room and recreation room, or in each crew cabin.
It explains the life-saving appliances and the best methods of survival, in easily understood terms and illustrated wherever possible.

It covers donning of lifejackets, immersion suits and thermal protective aids; muster at the assigned stations; boarding, launching and clearing the survival craft; the method of launching from within the craft; release from launching appliances.

It covers methods and use of devices for protection in launching areas; illumination in launching areas; use of all survival equipment; use of all detection equipment; illustrated instructions for the radio life-saving appliances.

It covers use of drogues, engine and accessories, recovery of survival craft, hazards of exposure and the need for warm clothing, best use of the survival craft facilities, methods of retrieval including helicopter rescue gear, and first aid.
It is in the working language of the ship.

technicalNotes.heading: What SOLAS III/36 requires the manual to contain
bullets: Instructions for on-board maintenance of the life-saving appliances, comprising: checklists for the inspections; maintenance and repair instructions; a schedule of periodic maintenance; a diagram of lubrication points with the recommended lubricants.
A list of replaceable parts; a list of sources of spare parts; and a log for records of inspections and maintenance.
It may be replaced by a shipboard planned maintenance programme that includes the same requirements, where the Administration permits.
It is ship-specific: a generic manual for a boat the ship does not have is a finding.
The log inside it is the evidence for SOLAS III/20 — the weekly and monthly inspections are recorded there or in the ship's log book.

technicalNotes.heading: Low-location lighting and signs
bullets: Escape routes are marked by signs and by low-location lighting, so the route is followable when smoke has filled the upper part of the space.
Photoluminescent material has to be charged by the ambient lighting; a sign in a compartment that is normally dark will be dark when you need it.
Signs are placed not more than the stated interval apart along the route and at every change of direction and at every door.
Markings are checked after every refit and every paint job — this is when they get covered.

technicalNotes.heading: Checking the route rather than the sign
bullets: Walk the escape route in the dark, from the deepest point outward, at least once in the maintenance cycle.
Look for stored gear, for doors that need a key, and for the point where the route crosses a fire zone boundary.
The route on the fire control plan and the route on the deck are supposed to be the same route.
A dogged escape hatch that needs two hands and a bar is an escape hatch that will not be used.

technicalNotes.heading: The second way out
bullets: A machinery space has two means of escape, and the trunk is usually the second one: a continuously enclosed fire-rated route to the open deck.
The trunk's doors, ladders and lighting are part of the escape and are inspected as such.
Nothing is stored in it. A trunk used as a locker is the finding that most often accompanies an incident report.
The upper exit opens from inside without a key and against the weather; test it, including in the ice season.
